before.label: West German historical social science / Sonderweg
before.description: Historical social science investigates German politics through social and economic structures. Wehler’s Empire interpretation, Kocka’s industrial and bourgeois research, and Frevert’s gender history address different questions. Fischer’s war-aims controversy is a related precursor.

strands.title: A journal as a research and discussion venue
strands.focus: The four authors of the 1975 foreword proposed combining historical interpretation with social-scientific analysis. Thematic issues, research reports and a discussion forum would connect specialists and wider readers. This is an announced programme, not proof that all editorial practice fulfilled it.

strands.title: Structural questions within inherited historical methods
strands.focus: Schieder reads Ranke, Droysen and other earlier historians as already addressing relations between individuals and larger forces. His call to revise inherited methods complicates an absolute divide between traditional history and structural inquiry; his portraits of rival traditions remain contestable.
strands.works: Strukturen und Persönlichkeiten, section I (1968 edition)

strands.title: Mentorship and political accountability
strands.focus: Wehler’s retrospective account combines intellectual gratitude to Schieder with discussion of Nazi-era writings and silence. The 1999 scholarly debate examines postwar continuities and the limits of earlier scrutiny. Methodological innovation and a liberal teaching style do not by themselves settle political responsibility.
strands.works: Wehler interview; Schulze, Helm and Ott on the historians’ debate (1999)

after.scope_note: A teaching umbrella spanning a research programme, a contested German-path argument and critics. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither is synonymous with the later Historikerstreit. Long-term conditions are not inevitable causes of Nazism, and gender history broadens the programme without making all contributors doctrinal adherents. Innovation also coexisted with inherited teaching relationships and politically contested continuities across 1945; the 1998–1999 debate over historians’ Nazi pasts is a distinct episode.

The checked publisher describes his analysis and Fischer-controversy setting. Direct reception of Ranke’s original work remains unproven. The 1975 journal programme explicitly combines historical-hermeneutic and social-scientific approaches. Schieder’s earlier section on structures and personalities also claims resources within older historiography. These primary texts qualify any reading of this criticism as an absolute methodological rupture; they do not verify direct Wehler reception of Ranke.

outcomes.finding: Complete 1975 founding foreword documents the journal as a concrete interdisciplinary discussion venue and identifies four collaborators. Schieder’s primary methodological section and Wehler’s teaching testimony show antecedents within older scholarship. Contemporary scholarly debate qualifies postwar renewal with political continuities, delayed scrutiny and contested mentor assessments. The journal/Schieder option resolves the bounded question; Rosenberg is not added from an unverified search lead.
outcomes.research_limit: Foreword read fully in 2010 reprint OCR, 91–94, with original 1975 pages 5–7 attributed. Programme is not proof of its implementation across journal history. Schieder section I read fully on reprint 137–144; later sections/endnotes unread and original edition not collated. His account of earlier authors remains an attributed interpretation. Wehler transcript selected mentoring, political-difference, teaching and Nazi-past passages read through the end of part 1; part 2 not fully read. Interview credits identify Hacke and Schäfer, 4 February 1999. Schulze/Helm/Ott opening and complete section I, selected section II and print citation read; remaining sections and underlying archives/chapters unread. Print citation confirms Deutsche Historiker im Nationalsozialismus (1999), 11–48. No independent audit of memoir claims, no exoneration through methodological novelty, and no conflation of 1998 debate with Historikerstreit. No image collation.
